That's right. The text says Jehoahaz "…did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his fathers had done." He was twenty-three when he became king, and he reigned three months. A short reign, and the verdict is already written.

explanations.answer: So he can't reign in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Yes, the text gives the reason plainly. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, imprisoned Jehoahaz at Riblah "…so that he could not reign in Jerusalem…" Nobody had to guess, because the verse hands it over.

explanations.answer: So he can serve in Egypt's army
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but the text never mentions an army. It says Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, imprisoned Jehoahaz at Riblah "…so that he could not reign in Jerusalem…" That's the reason the verse gives.

explanations.answer: So he can learn Egypt's ways
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have any lessons going on here. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, imprisoned Jehoahaz at Riblah "…so that he could not reign in Jerusalem…" That's the reason the verse gives. This was a lockup, not a training program.

That's the one. The text says Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, "…made Eliakim son of Josiah king in place of his father Josiah…" The one who made him king was Egypt's king. That's the whole answer the verse gives.

Not here. Earlier, the people of the land made Jehoahaz king (2 Kings 23:30), so you might expect Judah to pick again. But this time the text says Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, made Eliakim king. The elders aren't even in this verse.

The priests don't show up in this part of the story. The text says Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, "…made Eliakim son of Josiah king in place of his father Josiah…" Neco is the one the verse names. That's who made the next king.
Correct. The text says Neco "…took Jehoahaz and carried him off to Egypt…" Pharaoh Neco was Egypt's king. Jehoahaz went from prison at Riblah to Egypt.

explanations.answer: Lets him go back to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That would be a gentler ending, but the text doesn't give it. Jerusalem now had a new king, Jehoiakim, and the text says Neco took Jehoahaz and carried him off to Egypt. I think that's a heavy turn for a man who'd only been king three months.

Hamath is the land where Riblah sits, which is why it's in the story. But the text doesn't give Jehoahaz any job there. It says Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, took him and carried him off to Egypt. Governor is a nice title, but it isn't in the verse.
Yes. The text says Neco carried Jehoahaz off to Egypt, "…where he died." He was twenty-three when he became king. It's a sad ending, and the text states it plainly.

The text actually says it the other way. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, carried Jehoahaz off to Egypt, "…where he died." The verse puts his death in Egypt. I think this is one of the heavier lines in the passage.

Age is a good guess, but the text doesn't use it. Jehoiakim took the silver and gold from the people "…each according to his wealth." How much you owed depended on what you had, not how many birthdays you'd counted. The payment was for Pharaoh Neco, Egypt's king.

Tribe is a sensible guess, but the text doesn't say it. Jehoiakim taxed the land and took the silver and gold from the people "…each according to his wealth." The amount followed what a person had. The payment was for Pharaoh Neco, Egypt's king.

Right. The text says Jehoiakim "…became his vassal for three years…" A vassal is a king who answers to a stronger king. So the man Pharaoh Neco put on the throne now answers to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. New boss, same throne. Somebody update the org chart.

The text doesn't send him there. Egypt's Pharaoh Neco was the one who made Jehoiakim king, so it might seem natural. But when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, invaded, the text says Jehoiakim "…became his vassal for three years…" He served Babylon's king.

Yes. The text says he served for three years "…until he turned and rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar." Nebuchadnezzar was the king of Babylon. So Jehoiakim went from serving him to turning against him.

The text says the opposite. Jehoiakim was Nebuchadnezzar's vassal for three years, "…until he turned and rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar." Nebuchadnezzar was the king of Babylon. The serving stopped when the rebelling started.

Pharaoh Neco, Egypt's king, did put Jehoiakim on the throne, so it's an understandable guess. But the text says it plainly: "…the LORD sent…" these raiders. Neco isn't part of this verse. This time the sender is named, and it's the LORD.

Assyria isn't in this part of the story. The text says "…the LORD sent Chaldean, Aramean, Moabite, and Ammonite raiders against Jehoiakim…" That's the answer the verse gives. No Assyrian king gets credit here.

explanations.answer: Babylon had taken all his territory
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The king of Egypt did not march out of his land again "…because the king of Babylon had taken all his territory, from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River." That's a big stretch of land. The king of Babylon's reach was now much bigger.

explanations.answer: He had made peace with Judah
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention any peace deal. It says the king of Egypt did not march out of his land again "…because the king of Babylon had taken all his territory…" The reason was Babylon, not a handshake with Judah.

explanations.answer: A plague had struck his army
explanations.explanation: No plague is mentioned in this passage. The text gives the reason: "…the king of Babylon had taken all his territory, from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River." That's the territory the verse names. Nothing in it mentions his army getting sick.
